Input ID, direction, and a comma-separated list of joints that outline the strip centerline. The program calculates strip boundaries from adjacent centerlines and slab edges. Theory & Documentation

This section documents the mechanics implemented by the application, the numerical workflow used to create and solve the finite-element model, and the technical references supporting the formulation. The analysis is a linear-elastic plate-bending model for preliminary slab assessment and design support.

Part I: Engineering TheoryPart II: Coding TheoryPart III: References
Part I: Engineering Theory
1. Scope, coordinates, degrees of freedom, and sign convention

The slab middle surface lies in the global x-y plane. Each shell node has three active plate degrees of freedom: transverse displacement w, rotation θx, and rotation θy. The nodal vector for an element with n nodes is:

de=[w1θx1θy1⋯wnθxnθyn]T
Equation 1

where de is the element displacement vector, wi is the transverse displacement at node i, and θxi and θyi are nodal rotations. Q4 elements have n=4 and 12 element degrees of freedom; T3 elements have n=3 and 9 element degrees of freedom.

The formulation models plate bending and transverse shear. It does not include in-plane membrane degrees of freedom, drilling rotation, geometric nonlinearity, or nonlinear concrete cracking.
2. Material properties and section rigidity

Concrete is treated as homogeneous, isotropic, and linear elastic. If the user enters zero for the elastic modulus, the application calculates:

Ec=4500fc′
Equation 2

where Ec is the concrete elastic modulus in MPa and fc′ is the specified concrete compressive strength in MPa.

G=Ec2(1+ν)
Equation 3

where G is the elastic shear modulus and ν is Poisson's ratio.

Db=Ech312(1−ν2)[1ν0ν10001−ν2],Ds=κsGhI2,κs=56
Equation 4

where Db is the plate-bending constitutive matrix, Ds is the transverse-shear constitutive matrix, h is slab thickness, κs is the shear-correction factor, and I2 is the two-dimensional identity matrix.

3. Factored gravity loading
qu=Df(γch1000+qSDL)+LfqLL
Equation 5

where qu is factored pressure in kPa, Df and Lf are dead- and live-load factors, γc is concrete unit weight in kN/m³, h is slab thickness in mm, qSDL is superimposed dead load in kPa, and qLL is live load in kPa. The solver converts pressure to N/mm² before forming element nodal loads.

4. Q4 isoparametric Reissner-Mindlin element

Axis-aligned four-corner slab areas are subdivided into bilinear Q4 elements. Natural coordinates (ξ,η) range from −1 to +1. The interpolation functions are:

N1=14(1−ξ)(1−η),N2=14(1+ξ)(1−η),N3=14(1+ξ)(1+η),N4=14(1−ξ)(1+η)
Equation 6

where Ni is the shape function associated with node i, and ξ and η are natural coordinates. The same functions interpolate geometry, transverse displacement, and rotations.

J=∂(x,y)∂(ξ,η),[Ni,xNi,y]=J−1[Ni,ξNi,η]
Equation 7

where J is the isoparametric Jacobian, Ni,x and Ni,y are global derivatives, and Ni,ξ and Ni,η are natural-coordinate derivatives.

5. T3 constant-strain triangular Mindlin element

Nonrectangular polygons are triangulated by ear clipping and recursively refined. For a triangle with signed double area 2A, the linear shape-function derivatives are constant:

2A=(x2−x1)(y3−y1)−(x3−x1)(y2−y1) N1,x=y2−y32A,N2,x=y3−y12A,N3,x=y1−y22A N1,y=x3−x22A,N2,y=x1−x32A,N3,y=x2−x12A
Equation 8

where A is triangle area and (xi,yi) are node coordinates. The application evaluates the shear interpolation at the centroid using Ni=1/3.

6. Bending curvatures and transverse-shear strains
κ=[θx,xθy,yθx,y+θy,x]=Bbde,γ=[θx+w,xθy+w,y]=Bsde
Equation 9

where κ is the curvature vector, γ is the transverse-shear strain vector, Bb is the bending strain-displacement matrix, and Bs is the shear strain-displacement matrix.

M=Dbκ,V=Dsγ
Equation 10

where M=[M11,M22,M12]T contains bending and twisting resultants in N·mm/mm, and V=[V13,V23]T contains transverse-shear resultants in N/mm.

7. Element stiffness, numerical integration, and load vector
Ke=∫AeBbTDbBbdA+∫AeBsTDsBsdA
Equation 11

where Ke is element stiffness and Ae is element area. Q4 bending stiffness uses 2-by-2 Gauss integration, while Q4 shear stiffness uses reduced one-point integration to reduce shear locking. T3 bending and shear terms are integrated using the constant element fields.

fe=∫AeNwTqudA
Equation 12

where fe is the consistent element load vector and Nw contains the transverse-displacement shape functions. Uniform Q4 and T3 loads are distributed equally among the element's transverse nodal degrees of freedom.

8. Column and wall support springs
kz=Ec(AtLt+AbLb)
Equation 13

where kz is vertical translational stiffness, At and Ab are top and bottom support areas, and Lt and Lb are storey heights above and below the slab.

kθx=αEc(Ix,tLt+Ix,bLb),kθy=αEc(Iy,tLt+Iy,bLb)
Equation 14

where kθx and kθy are rotational spring stiffnesses, Ix,t, Ix,b, Iy,t, and Iy,b are effective section inertias, and α is 4 for a fixed far end or 3 for a pinned far end.

Ix=ψHB312,Iy=ψBH312
Equation 15

where B and H are rectangular section dimensions and ψ is the entered stiffness modifier. Wall stiffness is distributed to coincident mesh nodes using each node's tributary wall length.

9. Global assembly and conjugate-gradient solution
Kd=F
Equation 16

where K is the assembled global stiffness matrix, d is the global displacement vector, and F is the assembled load vector. Element terms and support springs are assembled by global degree-of-freedom indices.

r(k)=F−Kd(k),‖r(k)‖2‖F‖2≤εCG
Equation 17

where r(k) is the residual at iteration k, εCG is the entered convergence tolerance, and ‖⋅‖2 is the Euclidean norm. The solver uses diagonal preconditioning and blocks result generation if convergence is not achieved.

10. Result recovery and equilibrium

Element-center curvatures and shear strains are recovered from the solved nodal vector using Equation 9, and section resultants are calculated with Equation 10. The application also compares total applied load with the sum of column and wall spring reactions.

ΔR=Rcolumns+Rwalls−Papplied,eR=100ΔRPapplied
Equation 18

where ΔR is the reaction imbalance, Rcolumns and Rwalls are summed support reactions, Papplied is total applied load, and eR is equilibrium error in percent.

11. Wood-Armer-style directional design moments
M1,+=max(0,M11+|M12|),M2,+=max(0,M22+|M12|) M1,−=max(0,−M11+|M12|),M2,−=max(0,−M22+|M12|)
Equation 19

where M1,+ and M2,+ are positive bending demands for bottom reinforcement, M1,− and M2,− are negative bending demands for top reinforcement, and |M12| is the absolute twisting moment.

12. Flexural reinforcement demand
As=B−B2−4AMu2A−As,existing A=(ϕsfy)22α1ϕcfc′b,B=ϕsfyd,α1=0.85−0.0015fc′
Equation 20

where As is additional reinforcement area, Mu is the factored design moment in N·mm, As,existing is existing reinforcement, ϕs and ϕc are resistance factors, fy is steel yield strength, b=1000 mm is the design strip width used for per-metre reinforcement, and d is effective depth.

13. Design-strip aggregation
Mstrip(s)=∑i∈S(s)Mibi,Vstrip(s)=∑i∈S(s)Vibi
Equation 21

where s is station along the strip, S(s) is the set of selected elements at that station whose centroids fall inside the strip boundaries, Mi and Vi are directional element resultants, and bi is element width transverse to the strip. The displayed design-strip lines are centerlines; calculated strip boundaries remain based on adjacent centerlines and slab edges.

14. One-way shear resistance
Vc=ϕcλβfc′bwdv,β=max(0.05,2301000+dv),dv=max(0.9d,0.72h)
Equation 22

where Vc is concrete shear resistance, λ=1.0 is the normal-density factor, β is the size-effect term, bw is design-strip width, and dv is effective shear depth. The application caps fc′ at 8 MPa.

15. Punching-demand summary
Vf=|Rz|−qu(cx+d)(cy+d)
Equation 23

where Vf is estimated punching shear demand, Rz is the column vertical spring reaction, qu is factored slab pressure, and cx and cy are column dimensions. Rotational spring reactions provide approximate unbalanced moments about the global axes. The output is a demand summary, not a complete punching-resistance design.

16. CSA A23.3 live-load patterning for shell analysis

CSA A23.3:24 Clause 13.6.3 requires appropriate load patterns to determine the maximum values of all stress resultants at every section. The program therefore defines physical load panels independently of the Q4/T3 mesh and applies one multiplier to every shell assigned to a panel.

F(p)=FD+∑j=1npλj(p)FL,j
Equation 24

where F(p) is the global load vector for pattern p, FD is the factored permanent-load vector, np is the number of independently loadable physical panels, λj(p) is the live-load multiplier for panel j, and FL,j is the full factored live-load vector for panel j.

Ds=γch1000+qSDL,Ls=qLL,Ls≤0.75Ds
Equation 25

where Ds is specified dead load, γc is concrete unit weight, h is slab thickness in millimetres, qSDL is specified superimposed dead load, and Ls=qLL is specified live load. The program reports whether the Clause 13.8.4.2 load-ratio condition is met; the occupancy condition still requires engineering judgment.

The full-live-load case is always solved. When patterning is enabled, the default reduced multiplier is 0.75, and the generated set includes complementary checkerboards, alternating rows and columns, target-panel cases, support-adjacent cases, and one-sided support cases. Clause 13.8.4 is an elastic-frame provision used here as a regular-system benchmark; Clause 13.6.3 remains the governing shell-analysis requirement.

Kd(p)=F(p),Rmax=maxpR(p),Rmin=minpR(p)
Equation 26

where K is the common linear-elastic global stiffness matrix, d(p) is the displacement vector for pattern p, and R(p) is a recovered response. The stiffness matrix is assembled once and reused for all right-hand sides. Directional design moments and reinforcement demand are calculated within each complete load case before their envelopes are formed, avoiding nonconcurrent combinations of M11, M22, and M12.

17. Panel-influence superposition
KdD=FD,KdL,j=FL,j
Equation 27

where dD is the displacement response to factored permanent load and dL,j is the displacement influence response to full factored live load on physical panel j. The program solves Equation 27 once for dead load and once for each panel, rather than solving the complete global system separately for every generated pattern.

d(p)=dD+∑j=1npλj(p)dL,j
Equation 28

where d(p) is the reconstructed displacement vector for pattern p, np is the number of physical panels, and λj(p) is the panel multiplier. Equation 28 is exact for the current linear-elastic model because K is unchanged between gravity-load patterns. Each reconstructed pattern is checked against the original equilibrium equation. If its relative residual exceeds the selected CG tolerance, the program automatically performs a corrective CG solve using the reconstructed vector as its initial estimate.

18. Factored-case contour browsing

The Results contour can display a complete individual factored pattern case or a signed element-by-element maximum or minimum envelope.

Re,max=maxpRe(p),Re,min=minpRe(p)
Equation 29

where Re(p) is the selected result component for element e in complete factored load case p. Maximum and minimum contours are signed envelopes. Each envelope element records its governing factored case, while individual-case contours preserve the concurrent component set from the selected pattern.

Pattern-model limitation. Automatically generated panels require a rectilinear column grid and existing corner joints. Irregular bays, transfer structures, openings, fixed occupancy zones, and nonuniform live loads require user-defined panel polygons and engineering review. The generated patterns do not replace project-specific loading arrangements when those arrangements are known.
Engineering limitations. The model excludes cracking and tension stiffening, creep, shrinkage, reinforcement orthotropy, membrane action, geometric nonlinearity, material nonlinearity, explicit slab-column contact, drop panels, capitals, openings, staged construction, soil-structure interaction, and dynamic effects. Mesh sensitivity, support idealization, load path, sign convention, and design-code applicability require independent engineering review.
Part II: Coding Theory
1. Input and state layer
  • Visible dynamic tables are mirrored into hidden CSV text areas. The sync() function parses those records into the central model object M.
  • Material, load, geometric, mesh, support, and solver settings are read from named HTML controls. Global storey heights are automatically applied to every column record.
  • Undo, redo, local autosave, standalone HTML working-file export, and working-file import provide state persistence.
2. Validation and geometry layer
  • Validation checks duplicate or missing IDs, invalid references, zero-area polygons, nonpositive properties, overlapping slab areas, and incomplete support or design-strip definitions.
  • Four-corner axis-aligned rectangles are classified as Q4 regions. Other valid simple polygons are triangulated by ear clipping into T3 regions.
  • T3 triangles are recursively subdivided until the longest side satisfies the requested mesh limit or the refinement-depth guard is reached. Coincident coordinates are merged using the geometric tolerance.
3. Finite-element assembly layer
  • When CSA pattern loading is enabled, each shell centroid is mapped to one physical panel. The code assembles one permanent-load vector and one live-load basis vector per panel, generates auditable pattern definitions, reuses the common stiffness matrix, solves each right-hand side, and stores the governing pattern ID with each envelope quantity.
  • Each shell element forms a local bending-plus-shear stiffness matrix and a consistent gravity-load vector.
  • Local degree-of-freedom indices are mapped into sparse global matrix rows stored as JavaScript Map objects.
  • Column and wall translational and rotational springs are added directly to matching global diagonal terms.
4. Numerical solution layer
  • The sparse system in Equation 16 is solved with a diagonally preconditioned conjugate-gradient iteration.
  • The relative residual in Equation 17 is tracked against the user-selected tolerance. Nonconverged solutions are rejected.
  • Applied load and recovered spring reactions are compared using Equation 18 as an equilibrium diagnostic.
5. Recovery, design, and visualization layer
  • Element-center displacement, bending, twisting, shear, and reinforcement values are recovered after solution.
  • Design strips aggregate selected directional element resultants using Equation 21. Bending-moment and shear-force diagrams are generated as scalable SVG.
  • Contour plots use element polygons with a blue-to-red colour scale. Tooltips map pointer coordinates back to model coordinates and report the nearest element result set.
  • Flexural reinforcement, one-way shear, and punching-demand tables are generated from Equations 20, 22, and 23.
6. Performance-preserving numerical implementation
  • The optimized pattern solver retains the same physical panels, load cases, finite-element matrices, convergence tolerance, and result envelopes. It solves one dead-load basis response and one live-load influence response per physical panel, reconstructs every CSA pattern by linear superposition, and verifies each reconstructed pattern against the original global equilibrium equation.
  • If a reconstructed pattern does not satisfy the selected relative residual tolerance, a corrective conjugate-gradient solve is automatically performed from the superposed displacement estimate. Sparse panel vectors, double-precision typed arrays, and a reusable diagonal preconditioner are retained.
  • Progress redraws are throttled to approximately eight updates per second and force recovery is chunked into about twelve reporting intervals per load case. These controls affect only browser rendering frequency, not structural calculation content.
7. Reporting and persistence
  • The PDF feature prints the live Results and Theory sections using vector SVG and live MathJax content. It waits for MathJax typesetting and two browser animation frames before opening the print dialog.
  • Print CSS repeats table headers, prevents rows and key sections from splitting, scales graphics to letter-size pages, and hides interactive controls.
  • The working-file feature clones the current HTML document and rewrites the startup loader with the current input state, producing a standalone timestamped HTML file.
